question: Find the definition of overfitting, then calculate the gap between train_accuracy and val_accuracy for run R01 in the regularization experiments dataset.
answer: Overfitting occurs when a model's training accuracy is significantly higher than its validation accuracy, indicating the model learns the training data too well, capturing noise as if it were a pattern. Ways to reduce overfitting include collecting more training data, simplifying the model, regularization (L1 and L2 penalties that shrink weights; L1 can drive weights to exactly zero), early stopping, dropout for neural networks, feature selection and cross-validation to choose hyperparameters. Learning curves, which plot error against training set size, help diagnose whether a model suffers from high bias or high variance.

S3.title: Ml Model Diagnostics Handbook
S3.text:
1. Reading Learning Curves
A learning curve plots training error and validation error against the training set size. In a high-bias
model both errors are high and they converge close to each other; adding more data barely helps
because the model is too simple. In a high-variance model the training error is low and a large gap
separates it from the validation error; the validation error keeps falling as more data is added, so
collecting more data helps.
When a model is overfitting the first actions to try are a simpler model, stronger regularization,
more training data or early stopping.

S4.title: Ml Lecture Notes
S4.text: 3. Generalization, Overfitting and the Bias-Variance Tradeoff A model generalizes when it performs well on new data, not just on the data used for training. Overfitting happens when a model memorizes noise and idiosyncrasies of the training set: training error is very low but validation or test error is much higher. Underfitting happens when the model is too simple to capture the pattern, so both training and validation error are high. The bias-variance tradeoff explains this. Bias is the error caused by overly simple assumptions; high-bias models underfit. Variance is the sensitivity of a model to the particular training sample; high-variance models overfit. Total expected error is bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise. Increasing model complexity lowers bias but raises variance.

S5.title: Ml Reference Notes
S5.text: Feature: an input variable used by a model, for example a person's age. Label or target: the value the model should predict. Hyperparameter: a setting chosen before training, such as the learning rate, tree depth or number of neighbors k. Parameter: a value learned during training, such as the weights of linear regression. Epoch: one full pass through the training data. Batch size: the number of examples used for one gradient update. Learning rate: the step size of gradient descent. Regularization: a penalty that discourages overly complex models. L2 (ridge) shrinks weights; L1 (lasso) can set weights to zero. Overfitting: low training error but high validation error because the model memorized noise. Underfitting: high error on both training and validation data because the model is too simple. Bias: error from wrong or overly simple assumptions.
